title: Chapter 9
paragraphs: The Profits of Stock

Profits on capital rise and fall for the same reasons that wages do: whether the wealth of a society is growing or shrinking. But those reasons act on profits very differently from how they act on wages.

Adding capital is what raises wages, yet it tends to lower profit. When many rich merchants pour their capital into the same trade, competing against each other naturally drives that trade's profit down. And when capital increases the same way across all the different trades a society carries on, the same competition produces the same effect everywhere.

As I noted earlier, it is hard to pin down the average wage of labour even in one place at one time. Usually the best we can do is identify the most common wage. With profits on capital, even that is rarely possible. Profit fluctuates so wildly that someone running a particular trade often cannot tell you himself what his average annual profit is. It moves with every shift in the price of the goods he deals in, with the good or bad luck of both his rivals and his customers, and with a thousand other accidents that can strike goods whether they travel by sea or by land or simply sit in a warehouse. So profit varies not just from year to year but from day to day, almost from hour to hour. Working out the average profit across all the different trades in a great kingdom must be far harder still, and judging with any precision what it was in earlier or remote periods is flatly impossible.

Even if we cannot fix the average profit on capital with any precision, now or in ancient times, the interest rate on money gives us a rough idea of it. Take it as a rule: wherever a lot can be made by using money, a lot will usually be paid for the use of it, and wherever little can be made, less will usually be paid. So as the ordinary market interest rate in a country changes, we can be sure the ordinary profit on capital changes with it, falling as interest falls and rising as it rises. Tracking interest over time, then, can give us some sense of how profit has moved.

Under the 37th statute of Henry VIII, any interest above ten percent was declared illegal. Before that, it seems, more had sometimes been charged. In the reign of Edward VI, religious zeal banned interest altogether. But that ban, like every other of its kind, is said to have had no effect, and probably made the evil of usury worse rather than better. Henry VIII's statute was revived by the 13th statute of Elizabeth, chapter 8, and ten percent stayed the legal rate until the 21st statute of James I cut it to eight percent. Soon after the Restoration it dropped to six percent, and the 12th statute of Queen Anne brought it to five. All these statutory adjustments seem to have been very sensibly made. They appear to have followed the market rate rather than led it, matching the rate at which people of good credit usually borrowed. Since Queen Anne's time, five percent has been somewhat above the market rate rather than below it. Before the recent war, the government borrowed at three percent, and people of good credit in the capital and in many other parts of the kingdom borrowed at three and a half, four, and four and a half percent.

Since Henry VIII's time, the country's wealth and revenue have been steadily advancing, and the pace of that advance seems to have sped up gradually rather than slowed down. They have not just been moving forward but moving forward faster and faster. Over the same period wages have risen continually, while in most branches of trade and manufacturing, profits on capital have been falling.

It generally takes more capital to run a trade in a big town than in a country village. The large amounts of capital employed in every branch of trade, along with the many rich competitors, usually push the rate of profit lower in the town than in the village. But wages are generally higher in a big town. In a thriving town, those with large amounts of capital to employ often cannot find enough workers, so they bid against one another to hire as many as they can, which raises wages and lowers profits. In remote parts of the country there is often not enough capital to employ everyone, so the people bid against one another for work, which lowers wages and raises profits.

In Scotland the legal interest rate is the same as in England, but the market rate is somewhat higher. People of the best credit there rarely borrow below five percent. Even private bankers in Edinburgh pay four percent on their promissory notes, which can be cashed in whole or in part on demand. Private bankers in London pay no interest at all on money deposited with them. There are few trades that cannot be carried on with less capital in Scotland than in England, so the common rate of profit must be somewhat higher there. As I noted earlier, wages are lower in Scotland than in England. The country is not only much poorer, but the steps by which it is improving, for it clearly is improving, seem much slower and more halting. In France, the legal interest rate has not always been set by the market rate over the course of this century (see Denisart, article "Taux des Intérêts," volume 3, page 13). In 1720 interest was cut from the twentieth penny to the fiftieth, that is from five to two percent. In 1724 it was raised to the thirtieth penny, or three and a third percent. In 1725 it was raised again to the twentieth penny, or five percent. In 1766, under Mr. Laverdy's administration, it was reduced to the twenty-fifth penny, or four percent. The Abbé Terray later raised it back to the old rate of five percent. The supposed aim of many of these violent cuts in interest was to clear the way for cutting the interest on the public debt, an aim that was sometimes achieved. France today is perhaps not so rich a country as England, and though its legal interest rate has often been lower than England's, its market rate has generally been higher, because there, as elsewhere, people have several very safe and easy ways of getting around the law. British merchants who have traded in both countries have assured me that the profits of trade are higher in France than in England, and that is no doubt why many British subjects choose to put their capital to work in a country where trade is looked down on rather than in one where it is highly respected. Wages are lower in France than in England. When you cross from Scotland into England, the difference you notice in the dress and faces of ordinary people clearly signals the difference in their condition. The contrast is sharper still when you come back from France. France, though certainly richer than Scotland, does not seem to be moving forward as fast. People there commonly, even popularly, believe the country is going backwards, a belief that I think is mistaken even for France, but that no one could possibly hold about Scotland who sees the country now and saw it twenty or thirty years ago.

The province of Holland, by contrast, is a richer country than England relative to the size of its territory and its population. There the government borrows at two percent and private people of good credit at three. Wages are said to be higher in Holland than in England, and the Dutch, as everyone knows, trade on lower profits than anyone else in Europe. Some have claimed that Dutch trade is declining, and it may be true that certain particular branches of it are, but the overall signs clearly point to no general decline. When profit shrinks, merchants are quick to complain that trade is decaying, even though falling profit is the natural result of prosperity, of more capital being employed in a trade than before. During the recent war the Dutch captured the whole carrying trade of France, of which they still hold a very large share. The huge holdings they have in both French and English funds, about forty million in the latter, it is said, though I suspect that figure is considerably exaggerated, and the large sums they lend to private people in countries where interest is higher than at home, all show that their capital is overflowing, that it has grown beyond what they can profitably employ in their own country's proper business. But none of this shows that the business itself has shrunk. Just as a private man's capital, though built up in one trade, may grow beyond what that trade can absorb while the trade itself keeps growing, so may the capital of a whole nation.

In our North American and West Indian colonies, not only wages but the interest on money, and therefore the profits on capital, are higher than in England. In the various colonies both the legal and the market interest rate run from six to eight percent. High wages and high profits together, however, are things that almost never go hand in hand except in the special circumstances of a new colony. A new colony must always, for a while, have too little capital for the size of its territory and too few people for the size of its capital, more so than most other countries. They have more land than they have the capital to cultivate. So the capital they do have is applied only to the most fertile and best-placed land, near the coast and along navigable rivers. Such land is often bought for less than even its natural produce is worth. Capital used to buy and improve such land must yield a very large profit and so can afford to pay very high interest. Accumulating so fast in such a profitable use, the planter can expand his workforce faster than he can find people for it in a new settlement, so those he does find are very generously paid. As the colony grows, profits gradually fall. Once all the most fertile and best-placed land has been taken, less profit can be made by cultivating land that is poorer in both soil and location, and less interest can be paid on the capital used for it. Accordingly, in most of our colonies both the legal and the market interest rate have come down considerably over this century. As riches, improvement, and population have grown, interest has declined. But wages do not sink along with profits. Demand for labour rises as capital rises, whatever its profits, and even after profits fall, capital may not only keep growing but grow much faster than before. It is with industrious nations growing rich as it is with industrious individuals. A large amount of capital, even at small profits, generally grows faster than a small amount at great profits. Money, as the proverb says, makes money. Once you have a little, getting more is often easy. The hard part is getting that first little bit. The link between growing capital and growing industry, or growing demand for useful labour, I have partly explained already and will explain more fully later, when I deal with the accumulation of capital.

Gaining new territory, or new branches of trade, can sometimes raise profits, and with them the interest on money, even in a country that is rapidly growing rich. The country's capital is not enough for the whole surge of new business such acquisitions open up among the various people who share it, so it is directed only to those particular branches that pay the most. Some of what had been employed in other trades is necessarily pulled out of them and shifted into the new, more profitable ones. So in all those older trades, competition becomes less than before. The market is supplied less fully with many kinds of goods, their prices rise more or less, and this yields a greater profit to those who deal in them, who can therefore afford to borrow at higher interest. For some time after the recent war ended, not only private people of the best credit but some of the greatest companies in London regularly borrowed at five percent, having previously not paid more than four, or four and a half. The great gain of territory and trade from our acquisitions in North America and the West Indies fully explains this, without any need to suppose that the society's capital had shrunk. So much new business to be carried on by the old capital must necessarily have reduced the amount employed in a great many particular branches, where, with less competition, profits must have been higher. I will have occasion later to give the reasons that lead me to believe Great Britain's total capital was not reduced even by the enormous expense of the recent war.

When a society's total capital shrinks, or the funds meant to maintain industry shrink, it lowers wages but raises profits, and with them the interest on money. Because wages fall, the owners of whatever capital remains can bring their goods to market more cheaply than before, and because less capital is employed in supplying the market, they can sell them dearer. Their goods cost them less and fetch more, so their profits, swelled at both ends, can easily afford a large interest. The great fortunes so suddenly and easily made in Bengal and the other British settlements in the East Indies should convince us that in those ruined countries wages are very low and profits very high. The interest on money is correspondingly high. In Bengal, money is often lent to farmers at forty, fifty, and sixty percent, with the coming crop mortgaged for repayment. Just as the profits able to pay such interest must devour almost the whole of the landlord's rent, so such monstrous usury must in turn devour most of those profits. Before the fall of the Roman republic, usury of the same kind seems to have been common in the provinces under the ruinous rule of their proconsuls. The virtuous Brutus lent money in Cyprus at forty-eight percent, as we learn from Cicero's letters.

In a country that had gained the full measure of riches its soil, climate, and position relative to other countries allowed, and that could therefore go no further yet was not slipping backwards, both wages and profits would probably be very low. In a country fully peopled relative to what its territory could feed or its capital could employ, competition for work would be so fierce that wages would fall to the bare minimum needed to keep up the number of labourers, and since the country was already fully peopled, that number could never grow. In a country fully stocked relative to all the business it had to do, as much capital would be employed in each particular branch as the nature and scale of the trade would allow. So competition would be as intense everywhere as possible, and ordinary profit as low as possible.

But perhaps no country has ever yet reached this level of wealth. China seems to have been stationary for a long time, and probably acquired long ago the full measure of riches its laws and institutions allow. Yet that measure may be far below what the nature of its soil, climate, and position could permit under other laws and institutions. A country that neglects or scorns foreign trade, and lets foreign ships into only one or two of its ports, cannot do the same volume of business it could under different laws and institutions. And in a country where the rich, the owners of large capital, enjoy a good deal of security, but the poor, the owners of small capital, enjoy almost none and are liable to be robbed and plundered at any time by the lesser mandarins under the pretence of justice, the amount of capital employed across all the different branches of business can never match what the nature and scale of that business could allow. In every branch, the oppression of the poor must hand a monopoly to the rich, who, by cornering the whole trade for themselves, are able to make very large profits. Accordingly, twelve percent is said to be the common interest on money in China, and ordinary profits on capital must be high enough to pay this large interest.

A flaw in the law can sometimes push the interest rate far above what the country's wealth or poverty would otherwise call for. When the law does not enforce contracts, it puts all borrowers on nearly the same footing as bankrupts or people of doubtful credit in better-regulated countries. The uncertainty of getting his money back makes the lender demand the same usurious interest usually charged to bankrupts. Among the barbarous nations that overran the western provinces of the Roman empire, the keeping of contracts was for many ages left to the good faith of the parties themselves. Their kings' courts of justice rarely got involved. The high interest of those ancient times may perhaps be partly explained by this.

When the law bans interest altogether, it does not stop it. Many people have to borrow, and no one will lend without some payment for the use of their money, payment suited not only to what can be made by using it but to the difficulty and danger of evading the law. The high interest rates among all Muslim nations are explained by Montesquieu not by their poverty but partly by this and partly by the difficulty of recovering the money.

The lowest ordinary rate of profit must always be a bit more than enough to cover the occasional losses that every use of capital is exposed to. Only this surplus is net, or clear, profit. What is called gross profit often includes not only this surplus but also what is set aside to cover such extraordinary losses. The interest a borrower can afford to pay corresponds only to the clear profit. In the same way, the lowest ordinary rate of interest must be a bit more than enough to cover the occasional losses to which lending is exposed even when done with reasonable prudence. If it were not, only charity or friendship could ever be a motive for lending.

In a country that had gained its full measure of riches, where every particular branch of business held the greatest amount of capital it could employ, the ordinary rate of clear profit would be very small, and so the usual market interest that could be paid out of it would be so low that no one but the very wealthiest could live on the interest of their money. Everyone of small or middling fortune would have to manage the use of their own capital themselves. Almost every man would have to be a man of business, or take up some kind of trade. The province of Holland seems to be nearing this state. There it is unfashionable not to be in business. Necessity makes it usual for almost everyone to be, and custom everywhere sets the fashion. Just as it is ridiculous not to dress, so it is, to some degree, not to be employed like everyone else. As a man of a civil profession looks awkward in a camp or garrison, and is even in some danger of being scorned there, so does an idle man among men of business.

The highest ordinary rate of profit may be so high that, in the price of most goods, it swallows up the entire share that should go to the rent of the land, leaving only enough to pay for the labour of making them and bringing them to market, at the lowest rate labour can anywhere be paid, the bare subsistence of the worker. The worker must always have been fed in some way while doing the work, but the landlord may not always have been paid. The profits of the trade that the servants of the East India Company carry on in Bengal may be not far from this rate.

The proportion that the usual market interest rate ought to bear to the ordinary rate of clear profit necessarily shifts as profit rises or falls. In Great Britain, double the interest is what merchants reckon a good, moderate, reasonable profit, terms that I take to mean nothing more than a common, ordinary profit. In a country where the ordinary rate of clear profit is eight or ten percent, it may be reasonable for half of it to go to interest wherever business is done with borrowed money. The capital is at the borrower's risk, and he in effect insures it for the lender, so four or five percent may, in most trades, be both an adequate profit on the risk of that insurance and an adequate reward for the trouble of employing the capital. But the proportion between interest and clear profit might not be the same in countries where the ordinary rate of profit was a good deal lower or a good deal higher. If it were much lower, half of it perhaps could not be spared for interest, and more might be spared if it were much higher.

In countries fast advancing toward riches, the low rate of profit may, in the price of many goods, offset the high wages, letting those countries sell as cheaply as their less thriving neighbours, where wages may be lower.

In fact, high profits push up the price of work far more than high wages do. Take the linen manufacture, for example. If the wages of all the different workers, the flax-dressers, the spinners, the weavers, and so on, were each raised twopence a day, the price of a piece of linen would only need to go up by a number of twopences equal to the number of workers involved, multiplied by the number of days they worked on it. The part of the price that comes from wages would, through all the stages of manufacture, rise only in arithmetical proportion to this rise in wages. But if the profits of all the different employers of those workers were raised five percent, the part of the price that comes from profit would, through all the stages of manufacture, rise in geometrical proportion to this rise in profit. The employer of the flax-dressers, in selling his flax, would charge an extra five percent on the whole value of the materials and wages he advanced to his workers. The employer of the spinners would charge an extra five percent both on the raised price of the flax and on the spinners' wages. And the employer of the weavers would likewise charge five percent both on the raised price of the linen yarn and on the weavers' wages. In raising the price of goods, a rise in wages works like simple interest in piling up a debt. A rise in profit works like compound interest. Our merchants and master manufacturers complain loudly about the bad effects of high wages in raising prices and so cutting their sales at home and abroad. They say nothing about the bad effects of high profits. They are silent about the harm done by their own gains, complaining only of other people's.
